papers.title: inClinico Agent for clinical trial endpoint prediction and prospective evaluation
papers.abstract: High attrition rates across clinical drug development impose immense clinical and financial burdens, yet prospectively forecasting whether an individual trial will achieve its primary endpoint remains challenging. Here we present a machine-learning system that predicts clinical trial success across phases I-IV, independently modeling studies with efficacy versus safety/toxicity primary endpoints. To prevent lookahead bias and outcome leakage, models are trained on registration-time features, including target and mechanism-of-action precedent, drug modality and novelty, trial design and operational characteristics, and frozen literature-derived target-choice embeddings. Each prediction yields a continuous Predictive Trial Index (PTI) between 0 and 1 reflecting success probability. On a test set of trials initiated in 2021 or later, the efficacy model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.828 (95% CI 0.812-0.845; n = 2,347) and the safety/toxicity model reached 0.809 (95% CI 0.787-0.831; n = 1,485). These models are embedded in inClinico Agent, an agentic AI system integrating frontier large language models (LLMs) with deterministic scoring engines, retrieval tools and specialized clinical skills. We also introduce ClinBench, a prospective benchmark of 2,040 ongoing trials evaluated by inClinico Agent and five frontier LLMs, establishing a leakage-free foundation for tracking prospective predictive accuracy as trials reach completion.

papers.title: Generating Insights Into (Mis)Information About Measles Vaccination in Amsterdam Through Social Listening, the Netherlands, 2024
papers.abstract: Background HPV-vaccination prevents HPV-related cancers, but uptake remains suboptimal. In the Netherlands, a catch-up campaign invited 18-27-year-olds for an additional cost-free opportunity to initiate or complete their HPV-vaccination in 2023-2024, which led to 24% of this invited population getting vaccinated. As young adults increasingly seek health information online, understanding online questions, concerns and misinformation in response to the campaign may help improve future vaccination efforts. Supplemental to overall evaluation of the vaccination campaign, we piloted online social listening processes to generate an insight report for Public Health Service (PHS) Amsterdam. Objective This study piloted online social listening processes at the PHS Amsterdam to identify actionable insights into questions, concerns and misinformation surrounding the HPV-vaccination catch-up campaign among young adults. Methods Upon inventory of potential platforms and data sources, a retrospective online social listening analysis was conducted across the platforms Instagram, Facebook, and X, collecting data from PHS, the National Public Health Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM), the Dutch public broadcasting foundation (NOS), and LINDA.meiden sources from January 1, 2023, to June 1, 2024. Publicly available posts, comments, and engagement concerning HPV-vaccination were manually collected, and inductively coded. Themes were assessed for risk, based on expected potential harm and observed reach, and used to develop recommendations. Results A total of 821 posts and 5157 comments were collected and analysed. Ten recurring themes were identified across varying levels of risk. Two themes were classified as high risk: an information gap regarding the effectiveness of HPV-vaccination and concerns about the transparency on HPV-vaccine side effects. Three themes were classified as medium risk: questioning HPV-vaccine effectiveness under certain circumstances, reduced general vaccine trust following COVID-19, and accessibility issues related to vaccination locations and service times. Two themes were classified as neutral risk: questions regarding eligibility criteria for the campaign and calls for broader HIPV-prevention measures. Finally, three low risk themes concerned questions regarding HPV-vaccine brand specifics, campaign choices, and questions about scheduling or rescheduling HPV-appointments. Comments also referred to subsequent information sources, including reliable sources (public health institutes), false narratives and misinformation. Recommendations focused on addressing questions and information gaps (i.e. improving HPV risk perception and providing more detailed HPV-vaccine information), improving communication about HPV-vaccination, and reducing practical barriers to vaccination. Conclusions Manual social listening across selected online sources provided actionable insights into the public discourse during the HPV-vaccination catch-up campaign. Results mostly reflected questions, concerns and information gaps. Although some themes were critical of HPV-vaccination, false narratives and misinformation did not dominate the discourse. Recommendations aim to reduce practical barriers and address information needs. This pilot showed that online social listening can be effectively implemented even with limited resources.

papers.title: Auxiliary modalities add no detectable discrimination or calibration over structured EHR for 30-day COPD readmission: evidence from a leakage-audited MIMIC-IV cohort
papers.abstract: Background: Hospital readmission is a common and costly outcome in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Multimodal deep learning models combining structured electronic health record (EHR) data with physiological, imaging, and textual data have been proposed to improve its prediction, but whether such fusion outperforms EHR data alone, once temporal-leakage safeguards are applied, remains unclear. Methods: Using a stratified MIMIC-IV cohort of COPD patients enriched to about 50% readmission (natural prevalence 18.1%; n=1,279; 895/192/192 training/validation/test), we predicted 30-day, all-cause readmission from four frozen, pre-trained encoders (electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, clinical notes, structured EHR). We audited and corrected temporal leakage in the admission-linkage pipeline of each modality, then compared three fusion architectures (naive concatenation, scalar gated fusion, EHR-anchored residual fusion) against unimodal baselines and an EHR-alone reference, using bootstrap significance testing, a missingness stress test, and calibration analysis with and without post-hoc recalibration. Results: The audit corrected three previously undetected temporal-alignment issues, affecting 5-9% of patients for clinical notes, 29-43% for chest radiographs, and 53-58% for ECG. After correction, every modality except EHR showed near-chance discrimination alone (ROC-AUC 0.46-0.53), confirmed with a non-linear adapter probe. No fusion architecture significantly outperformed the EHR-alone baseline (ROC-AUC 0.63); removing auxiliary modalities improved rather than degraded fusion performance under stress testing. The raw Brier score was lower for all three fusion architectures than for EHR-alone (about 0.24 versus 0.32), but this reflected overconfidence of the EHR-alone probe (calibration slope 0.12); after logistic recalibration fitted on the validation set, Brier scores were indistinguishable (EHR-alone 0.239; fusion 0.240-0.244; all paired bootstrap 95% CIs included zero). Conclusions: Structured EHR data alone matched the discrimination and, after recalibration, the calibration of more complex multimodal fusion for 30-day COPD readmission prediction. These findings highlight the importance of rigorous temporal-leakage auditing in multimodal clinical prediction research and suggest that reformulating this task around temporal proximity to the outcome, rather than refining the fusion mechanism further, may be more productive for future work.

papers.title: Instability as Signal: Diagnosing Latent Heterogeneity in Multimodal Survival Models
papers.abstract: Survival prediction frequently exhibit unstable and irreproducible performance, limiting their clinical applicability. Rather than proposing a new predictive architecture, this work presents a diagnostic investigation into the sources of this instability. Using a transformer-based deep fusion model combining RNA sequencing and histopathology data from the TCGA-BRCA cohort as a diagnostic probe, we demonstrate that global survival prediction is highly unstable across data splits. We then analyze the learned multimodal embeddings in an unsupervised manner, revealing stable latent patient subgroups with significantly divergent survival outcomes. These subgroups are not explained by canonical receptor status or immune infiltration, but instead align with tumor-intrinsic proliferative activity. Conditioning survival modeling on the largest discovered subgroup recovers strong and stable prognostic performance, substantially outperforming unimodal baselines. These findings indicate that survival predictability is conditional on latent heterogeneity and suggest that heterogeneity-aware modeling strategies are essential for robust multimodal prognostication. This work establishes a methodological framework for interpreting instability in multimodal survival learning.

papers.title: Introducing Infrastructure as Code for deployment and governance of medical AI: A case study
papers.abstract: Clinical AI deployment rarely reaches the bedside because both workstation integration and governed backend provisioning are challenging. We introduce a workflow that allows rapid and governed access to AI functionalities through a browser interface or API, enabling privacy-compliant data analysis. The complex setup for compliant healthcare applications such as a secure backend, private AI model endpoint, and managed identity configuration is encoded by itself, a concept known as Infrastructure as Code (IaC). IaC is a concept in which networks, access rights, and service endpoints are written down as machine-readable files that can be reviewed once and executed identically in any institution. Here, we apply this concept to a clinical use case. The process of deploying a governed, private clinical AI solution using this approach in a tertiary care center took, on average, 310.3 +- 196.6 seconds (n=25, mean +- SD). To further demonstrate the clinical value of this approach, we developed and deployed an LLM-based inconsistency checker, which identifies textual inconsistency in medical documents. When evaluating the tool on a set of 1,347 physician-approved clinical documents, the tool flagged a clinically severe inconsistency in 105 clinical documents (7.8%, approximately 1 in 13). In a severity-stratified physician audit, 149 of 150 sampled findings were confirmed (population-weighted PPV 98.2%; CI 94.8 - 100.0). In summary, we present the application of IaC frameworks to a healthcare use case and demonstrate that clinically useful AI applications can be deployed to physician workstations in hospital-governed cloud environments within a few minutes.

papers.title: Provider Experiences with AI Clinical Decision Support in eSanjeevani
papers.abstract: Background: Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) are increasingly embedded in national telemedicine services, however how different stakeholders who use them experience these tools, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, is less explored. In the assisted model of India's eSanjeevani service, spoke health workers enter structured symptoms and hub clinicians review a symptom summary and an artificial intelligence (AI)-generated differential diagnosis. Objective: To describe role-specific experiences of eSanjeevani's CDSS functions and to estimate how acceptance coexists with specific reported difficulties within each role. Methods: We analyzed a program feedback web survey completed between 11 July and 29 July, 2025 by hub clinicians and spoke providers. Prespecified item profiles covered review of summaries and suggested diagnoses, the perceived relation of suggestions to the clinician's own diagnosis, ease of use and intention to use (hub), and symptom-capture utility, question quantity, question relevance, summary presentation and satisfaction (spoke). Within-role contrasts were reported as absolute differences in acceptance with Newcombe 95% CIs. Short open comments underwent content analysis. Results: The cohort comprised 190 hub and 662 spoke respondents from 13 and 15 states (21.4% and 19.3% of eligible providers). Among hub respondents, 76.8% regularly reviewed the symptom summary and 58.9% the suggested diagnoses; 72.6% judged suggestions matched (32.6%) or appropriate but different (40.0%), 7.9% mostly inappropriate, and 11.1% reported that suggestions were mostly not generated. Overall, 85.3% intended to keep using the tools. Affirmative intention was 98.4% when suggestions matched, 66.7% when they were mostly inappropriate (difference vs matched or appropriate -23.2 percentage points, 95% CI -48.5 to -4.0) and 61.9% when mostly absent (-25.7, 95% CI -47.1 to -7.3); technical issues, reported by 38.4%, made little difference (-2.8, 95% CI -14.1 to 7.3). Among spoke respondents, 63.4% rated question quantity appropriate, with miscalibration in both directions (15.6% too many; 16.6% too few); 89.9% found the questions relevant and 91.8% found the summary clear. Satisfaction was 75.3% and did not differ materially between those reporting too many questions and those reporting an appropriate number (-2.7, 95% CI -12.8 to 6.0). Comments located spoke difficulties in question burden and missing complaints, and hub difficulties in freezing and in the scope and availability of suggestions. Estimates were stable across cohort, ambiguity and state-exclusion sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: Acceptance of eSanjeevani's CDSS was high in both roles. For hub clinicians it tracked the perceived quality and availability of AI suggestions rather than technical friction; spoke workers accepted the question burden, but its two-directional miscalibration points toward complaint-specific, adaptive questioning. These provider reports do not measure diagnostic accuracy. They identify log-based and audit-based indicators that the next evaluation cycle should measure directly.

papers.title: Patient Needs and Requirements for a Decision Aid Navigator System (DEAN) Patient Portal: A Qualitative Study
papers.abstract: Background: Patient Decision aids (PtDAs) are important tools that support shared decision-making (SDM) between clinicians and patients, enabling patients to be more informed and engaged in decisions regarding their care. The use of PtDAs can increase patient knowledge, reduce decisional regret, and engage the clinician and patient in meaningful dialogue. Shared decision-making relies on decision aids, but how patients receive the PtDA can vary. This qualitative study elucidated patient familiarity with PtDAs and the barriers, needs, and requirements of patients to access and confidently use DAs, including when received via a clinician-facing EHR-integrated Decision Aid Navigator System (DEANS). Methods: We conducted six focus groups (FG) with participants who were recruited from two academic medical centers. Focus groups included an introduction to what a PtDA is and an exploration of how patients or family members, i.e., people who had not made a medical decision for themselves using a PtDA, but who have helped a family member, had previously used PtDAs in their healthcare. The FGs focused on PtDA-users, affordances and barriers to using PtDAs, and PtDA-user needs and requirements of a proposed DEAN patient portal. We applied Rapid Qualitative Analysis (RQA) to summarize the data, using a consensus making approach to identify emerging themes. Results: We identified three overarching themes: 1) Patients had varied familiarity with PtDAs and often confused them with general health tools, but found value in SDM, 2) Patients perceived technology accessibility, PtDA credibility, and time as barriers potentially impeding PtDA use, and 3) Patients valued flexible, user-friendly, and accessible PtDAs that support patient-led decisions, particularly when introduced by clinicians and delivered via a patient portal. Conclusion: This study provides patient-derived insights into factors that influence PtDA uptake, highlighting common misconceptions about PtDAs and identifying key patient priorities such as accessibility, flexibility, clear content, and clinician-guided usage. Patient also expected clinicians to be familiar with PtDAs, especially when the PtDA covers a complex decision. These findings can inform the development of more patient-centered SDM infrastructure and strategies to support PtDA use in clinical practice, including clinician-supported delivery, accessibility, and integration into routine care to strengthen shared decision-making.

papers.title: Effects of Dish Name, Visible Amount, Persona, and Explicit Instruction on Energy Estimates From Food Photographs by 26 Vision-Language Models: Comparative Evaluation Study
papers.abstract: Background: Vision-language models (VLMs) are being considered for estimating energy intake from meal photographs. Prompt descriptions such as a Japanese-dietitian persona shift the estimates, suggesting their use for calibration; what the estimates rest on was unknown. Objective: We examined whether prompt descriptions can serve as calibration, at which training stage responses to a nationality persona and to an amount instruction arise, and whether estimates follow the visible amount or one associated with the identified dish. Methods: Eleven commercial and 15 open-weight models were evaluated on NutriImage (887 Japanese single-dish photographs) and SNAPMe (1,134 US meal photographs) under eight prompt conditions (no description, five personas, and smaller- or larger-portion instructions). With one model, images were cropped or replaced by the dish name. Before- and after-meal photographs of 804 meals (ACETADA) were estimated. Pre-trained and post-trained weights of Gemma 3 and InternVL3.5 8B were compared by likelihood scoring. Prompts were compared with numerical calibration. Results: Where the dish was named as in the full image, a 25% crop changed neither the median absolute percentage error (MedAPE; 33.8% vs 34.4%) nor the persona shift (-20 vs -20 kcal); dish names alone gave similar accuracy (MedAPE 31.7%); nearly empty trays still received 39%-75% of the before-meal estimate, often described as already eaten. Between models, the persona shift was related to baseline bias (r = -0.77) and less to instruction following (r = -0.36); the instruction shift showed the reverse (r = -0.14 and -0.95). In Gemma 3, the Japan-US contrast was 2-4 times larger before post-training, and the instruction response 2-4 times larger after it (InternVL3.5 8B: 3 and 1.4 times). Across images, the Japan-US contrast was uniform on US meals and, for Japanese dishes in the commercial models, Gemma 3, and Qwen3-VL 32B, larger where overestimated. In these models, the persona lowered MedAPE for Japanese dishes as much as, or slightly more than, subtracting the mean bias, and no more than dividing by a ratio; on US meals it did not; in open-weight families that responded little, only numerical calibration lowered error. The smaller-portion instruction raised MedAPE in models with little bias (eg, 30.0% to 50.2%). Conclusions: In the model examined most closely, the estimates behaved as if anchored on an amount associated with the identified dish and only partly corrected by the visible amount. Prompt descriptions moved them by amounts depending on model and cuisine, not on the correction needed; a persona is therefore not proposed as a general means of calibration. In a facility, the findings suggest showing the identified dish for correction, calibrating by a ratio measured on reference meals with the deployed model, keeping amount statements out of the prompt, and not deriving intake from before-after-meal differences.

papers.title: AI-assisted identification of potential treatment injury from inpatient discharge summaries: an early-stage sociotechnical evaluation in a New Zealand district hospital
papers.abstract: Objectives: To assess the feasibility and early performance of an AI-assisted screening workflow that reviews inpatient discharge summaries to identify potential treatment injuries for clinician review and, where appropriate, Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) treatment injury claim consideration in New Zealand. Design: Single-site, six-month pilot reported as a quality-improvement/service-evaluation activity. A large language model (LLM)-enabled system acted as an index screening test over discharge summaries to generate candidate treatment injury signals for structured clinician adjudication and escalation. Setting: A New Zealand district hospital (Wairarapa). Screening operated on routinely produced inpatient discharge summaries. Participants: All inpatient discharge summaries produced during the pilot period were screened (n = 2,642). The unit of analysis was one discharge summary per inpatient episode. Intervention: An LLM-based screening workflow that outputs structured candidate harm signals with supporting excerpts and a certainty label. Outputs were reviewed by clinicians using a structured adjudication template. Suitable cases could be escalated to senior clinicians and followed through the local ACC treatment injury process. Main outcome measures: Primary outcomes were yield, positive predictive value (PPV) of AI- flagged signals for clinician-adjudicated iatrogenic harm, and the rate of unsupported/hallucinated outputs. Secondary outcomes included overlap with incident reporting and administrative coding, downstream ACC claim outcomes, and clinician review workload. Results: Across 2,642 inpatient discharge summaries screened, the AI-assisted workflow generated 237 candidate signals (yield 9.0%; 95% CI 7.9% to 10.1%). Clinician adjudication classified 102 as confirmed iatrogenic harm, 43 as possible harm requiring additional context, 81 as no harm, and 11 as unsupported/hallucinated outputs. PPV for confirmed harm was 43.0% (95% CI 36.8% to 49.4%). PPV for confirmed-or-possible harm was 61.2% (95% CI 54.9% to 67.1%). Seven ACC treatment injury claims were lodged as a direct result of AI-assisted surfacing; three were accepted, two declined, and two were held/pending at analysis. Organisational ACC data identified 68 treatment injury claims lodged during the same period, of which 17 overlapped with AI-identified cases. Conclusions: AI-assisted screening of discharge summaries can feasibly increase detection of potential treatment injuries for structured clinician review and may support more systematic ACC consideration and safety learning. Safe scaling requires transparent reporting of model and prompt details, robust human adjudication and escalation pathways, and governance controls to mitigate false positives and unsupported outputs. A next-stage evaluation should estimate diagnostic accuracy against a chart-review reference standard and examine implementation outcomes including workload, acceptability, fidelity and sustainability.

papers.title: Cross-database adaptation of machine learning models for predicting sustained antibiotic exposure among patients with intracerebral hemorrhage in intensive care units
papers.abstract: Background: Patients with intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in intensive care units (ICUs) frequently receive antibiotics early in critical illness. Such exposure reflects suspected infection, physiological deterioration, monitoring intensity, and clinical management and may vary across institutions and electronic health record databases. We evaluated target-domain adaptation for modeling sustained antibiotic exposure in critically ill patients with ICH. Methods: We analyzed derived ICH cohorts from MIMIC-IV and the eICU Collaborative Research Database. MIMIC-IV included 2,024 ICU stays and served as the source cohort. The eICU cohort comprised 1,277 stays and was divided, at the ICU-stay level, into a development subset (766 stays) and a held-out evaluation subset (511 stays). The eICU outcome was sustained antibiotic exposure on at least two ICU days. Candidate models incorporated demographic, comorbidity, physiological, laboratory, neurologic, respiratory, temporal, and measurement-process features. Timestamped observations for static and temporal tabular families were censored at the recorded first-antibiotic time when available, whereas the compact sequence component and explicit measurement-density features used the full first 24 hours. For base-model families using eICU development data, meta-learner inputs were generated by five-fold stratified cross-fitting. A 42-input L2-penalized logistic meta-learner combined 16 model probabilities with model-summary, clinical, availability, and measurement-density features. Results: The held-out eICU subset contained 48 positive outcomes (9.39%). The adapted ensemble achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.841 (95% CI 0.775-0.899) and an average precision (AP) of 0.540 (95% CI 0.399-0.676), with a Brier score of 0.063 and expected calibration error of 0.029. The MIMIC-IV source-only stack achieved an AUROC of 0.782; the paired AUROC difference was 0.059 (95% CI 0.003-0.112). In a separate patient-grouped five-fold out-of-fold sensitivity analysis of 503 linked eICU stays, AUROC was 0.807 (95% CI 0.691-0.910). Conclusions: Target-domain adaptation improved held-out discrimination relative to a source-only stack for sustained antibiotic exposure. Because some model components and measurement-process features used information from the broader first 24 hours, the model should be interpreted as a first-24-hour treatment-association model rather than a strictly prospective pre-treatment infection predictor.

papers.title: Development and Cross-Database External Validation of 24-Hour Landmark Models for ICU Mortality After Intracerebral Hemorrhage: Incremental Value of Routine Coagulation Markers
papers.abstract: Background: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is associated with high early mortality. Although routine coagulation markers are clinically relevant, their incremental value for mortality prediction beyond neurologic and physiologic information is uncertain. We developed and externally validated models using first-24-hour ICU data and evaluated the added predictive value of routine coagulation measurements. Methods: We used MIMIC-IV for model development and eICU-CRD for external validation. The development cohort included 2,669 adults with non-traumatic ICH and 388 ICU deaths. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were evaluated using a patient-level 70:30 holdout split and 5-fold stratified cross-validation. External validation used a high-specificity primary eICU cohort (396 patients; 39 deaths) and a broader secondary hemorrhagic-stroke/likely-ICH cohort (1,555 patients; 168 deaths). Performance was assessed using AUROC, AUPRC, Brier score, calibration, and paired bootstrap comparisons. GCS-only and age-plus-GCS models served as clinical benchmarks. Coagulation-only, clinical-only, and combined XGBoost models were compared to assess incremental value. Results: In the internal holdout cohort, AUROCs were 0.870 for logistic regression, 0.859 for random forest, and 0.867 for XGBoost. In the primary external cohort, corresponding AUROCs were 0.804, 0.839, and 0.817; AUPRCs were 0.342, 0.419, and 0.406; and Brier scores were 0.080, 0.072, and 0.074. In the broader cohort, AUROCs were 0.826, 0.848, and 0.838. Random forest showed the numerically strongest external performance, but pairwise AUROC differences among multivariable models were not clearly supported. GCS-only achieved AUROCs of 0.780 and 0.813 in the primary and broader cohorts. Coagulation-only XGBoost showed weak discrimination (AUROC 0.598 internally, 0.598 primary external, and 0.566 broader external). Adding coagulation variables to the clinical model produced AUROC differences of 0.014 (95% CI -0.009 to 0.037) and 0.003 (95% CI -0.007 to 0.013) in the two external cohorts. Conclusions: Multivariable models based on first-24-hour ICU data retained useful discrimination across external cohorts and provided modest gains over simple GCS-based benchmarks. Routine coagulation markers alone were weak predictors and did not provide clearly supported incremental discrimination beyond broader clinical information. Cross-database transportability should be interpreted together with phenotype alignment and calibration.

papers.title: Development and Evaluation of an Offline Vision-Language Model System for Estimating Nutrients from Meal Photographs on Personal Devices: The PLANS (Personal-device Local Assessment of Nutrients System) Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundEstimating nutrient intake from meal photographs with vision-language models (VLMs) is now practical, but patient photographs often cannot leave the institution. We developed PLANS (Personal-device Local Assessment of Nutrients System), in which a small open VLM runs entirely on a personal device. MethodsOpen VLMs were compared on two image sets with reference values (NutriImage, 887 Japanese meals; SNAPMe, 1,134 US meals), and the selected model (Qwen3-VL-4B, 4-bit) was run on an iPad Air without network access. Energy (primary outcome), protein, fat, carbohydrate and salt were evaluated by median absolute percentage error (MedAPE) and Spearmans {rho}. The effect of supplying the food weight, including errors in it, was examined. ResultsEnergy estimates on the iPad were identical to those of a desktop-computer run for 84-86% of images (other values, 75-87%). MedAPE on the iPad was 37.0% and 36.5% for energy (26-28% of images within {+/-}20%), 43-65% for the macronutrients and 68-101% for salt ({rho} 0.51-0.85). On the desktop computer, supplying the true weight reduced MedAPE of the 4B model on NutriImage from 37.0% to 32.5% for energy and from 100.0% to 66.8% for salt; energy MedAPE stayed below the base value for declared weights of 0.5-1.25 times the true weight or rounded to 50 g, but rose markedly when the container weight was included. ConclusionsAn offline VLM on a tablet reproduced server-side energy accuracy and is a candidate tool for dietary counselling where photographs cannot leave the institution; given the wide limits of agreement, its usefulness in practice remains to be examined.

papers.title: NESTApp: A GUI-Based MATLAB Application for Auditable TMS-EEG Preprocessing with EEGLAB
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) preprocessing determines signal quality and interpretation, particularly for transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with EEG (TMS-EEG), where recordings are affected by large and complex stimulation-related artifacts. Several preprocessing approaches have been developed, but substantial variability remains in how pipelines are implemented, documented, and evaluated across recordings, limiting reproducibility and comparability across studies. We developed NESTApp, a MATLAB-based graphical interface built on EEGLAB, to provide an accessible and reproducible framework for implementing and evaluating TMS-EEG preprocessing pipelines. Rather than prescribing a specific pipeline, NESTApp allows users to construct and consistently apply customisable workflows incorporating established EEGLAB and TMS-EEG processing tools, while automatically documenting processing decisions and parameters. Integrated quality-control procedures track data removal and flag recordings based on user-defined criteria, facilitating systematic evaluation across participants. The application also supports group-level visualisation and export of processed TMS-EEG measures for subsequent analyses. Applied to 29 recordings from 16 participants, NESTApp processed 27 and identified those requiring further inspection. By integrating pipeline implementation, documentation, quality control, and group-level evaluation within a single interface, NESTApp provides a transparent framework for TMS-EEG preprocessing that may improve reproducibility, facilitate consistent processing across cohorts, and lower technical barriers to the implementation of established preprocessing approaches.

papers.title: AI chatbots abandon sleep apnoea referral when simulated patients minimise symptoms
papers.abstract: BackgroundPatients increasingly consult free artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots about their symptoms, but these models may favour agreement with the patient over accuracy. In obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), where most cases in the general population remain undiagnosed and diagnosis depends on referral, this could validate symptom denial. We tested whether consumer chatbots maintain guideline-concordant referral when a simulated patient minimises symptoms. MethodsSeven guideline-concordant and standardised OSA vignettes (apnoea-hypopnoea-index, AHI 8-52 events/h; body mass index 28-42 kg/m2) were presented to five free chatbots (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash and Grok-4.3) under neutral and symptom-minimising conditions (10 simulated conversations per model- vignette-condition cell; N=700). Referral maintenance was scored by a structured rubric and every capitulation was human-confirmed. ResultsAll chatbots maintained referral recommendations in neutral conversations (350/350; 100%). When simulated patients minimised symptoms and resisted referral, maintenance fell to 64.3% (225/350), a reduction of 35.7 percentage points (95% CI 5.5- 66.0; p=0.028). Rates ranged from 55.7% to 85.7% across chatbots, but evidence of between-chatbot differences was inconsistent across analyses. Rates differed across clinical vignettes (p=0.001). A variance analysis estimated greater variation between vignettes than between chatbots. In the three driving-risk vignettes, referral recommendations were abandoned in 46- 68% of symptom-minimising conversations, pooling all five chatbots within each vignette. ConclusionsConsumer AI chatbots abandoned correct OSA referral recommendations in about one-third of symptom-minimising conversations, with higher observed abandonment in simulated cases involving driving risk. This may delay appropriate assessment and raises patient- and public-safety concerns.

papers.title: The content of biomedical papers predicts future clinical trials: a proof-of-concept framework tested on CAR-T cell therapy
papers.abstract: This paper shows that it is possible to predict which newly published biomedical research papers will be connected to subsequent clinical trials. We use CAR-T cell therapy as a proof-of-concept setting because its development can be followed from published research through clinical testing, regulatory approval, and commercialization. We reconstructed connections between research papers and clinical trials and trained machine-learning models to predict which papers were associated with research that progressed to clinical testing. Using 65 paper-inherent indicators, including scientific topic, language, biomedical orientation, and team structure, the models achieved a cross-validated AUC of 0.908. The resulting rankings were also practically informative. In a retrospective analysis using no information generated after 2016, 80% of the top 20 papers came from laboratories associated with one of 13 predefined major CAR-T clinical or commercial outcomes. As an additional finding, first-year citations alone achieved an AUC of 0.797, while provenance indicators based on author, journal, and institutional reputation performed less strongly and added little to the paper-inherent model. Our results show that whether biomedical research papers will be connected to subsequent clinical trials can be predicted from newly published papers with high discrimination in CAR-T. Our findings could help research organizations and pharmaceutical companies identify papers, laboratories, and therapeutic programs that warrant closer evaluation before clinical outcomes are known.

papers.title: Label-free, low-cost AI ranking for systematic review screening
papers.abstract: Title and abstract screening is among the most labor-intensive steps of systematic reviews. Jev, a low-cost AI decision model, scores records against eligibility criteria without screening labels. We scored 169,982 records from 128 reviews and, after tuning on development reviews, evaluated 23 held-out reviews once and 31 Cochrane reviews post hoc. Jev outranked the best free ranker in all 23 held-out reviews (mean AUC 0.966 vs 0.831) and came within 0.011 AUC of Claude Opus 5.5 on 1999 records at about 1/700 of its list-price cost (US$0.02/1000 records). Combined with active learning, it raised work saved at 95% recall from 0.659 to 0.806. A fixed score threshold fell below 95% recall in 3 of 28 Cochrane reviews, whereas Jev ranking with statistical stopping (post hoc) reached 95% recall in all 51 reviews, reading 86-88% of records. Label-free ranking with Jev was accurate and inexpensive, but stopping safely required screening decisions.

papers.title: Decision models can offload structured clinical tasks from large language models
papers.abstract: Decision models like Jev read text and return probabilities, categories, or ordinal levels, with confidence scores for the latter two, at a fraction of large language models (LLMs) cost. We explored how Jev could be integrated into clinical workflows for all these output types: mortality risk estimation, categorical Choosing-Wisely decisions for patient questions, and ordinal colon cancer staging. With standard LLM-style inputs, Jev trailed five flagship LLMs: mortality AUROC was 0.822 versus 0.837-0.846; Choosing-Wisely accuracy, 87.7% versus 98.4-100%; and staging accuracy, 45.4% versus 94.2-100%. Developer-recommended input alterations improved staging accuracy to 75.8% with medical context, 82.1% with task decomposition, and 85.8% with both. None of Jevs staging errors had full confidence. Using Jev for fully confident staging decisions and LLMs for the rest was non-inferior to each LLM alone and cut flagship LLM costs by 33-44%. Prompted as designed, decision models may efficiently share structured clinical tasks with LLMs.

papers.title: ClinStigma: A Clinician-Guided Framework for Developing Synthetic Benchmarks of Contextual Stigmatizing Language in Clinical Documentation
papers.abstract: ObjectiveLarge language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate, summarize, and evaluate clinical documentation, yet standardized methods for evaluating nuanced, context-dependent clinical language remain limited. Existing approaches rely primarily on annotated clinical corpora or keyword-based methods, restricting reproducibility, public dissemination, and systematic comparison across models. We present ClinStigma, a clinician-guided framework for constructing, annotating, and evaluating synthetic benchmarks of contextual stigmatizing language, demonstrated through ClinStigma-SUD, its inaugural implementation for substance use disorder documentation. Materials and MethodsCandidate clinical sentences were generated using a frontier language model and iteratively reviewed according to a clinician-developed annotation rubric refined through expert review in stigmatizing language. The resulting benchmark intentionally incorporates explicit stigmatizing, neutral, and contextually ambiguous ("gray-zone") documentation requiring clinical reasoning rather than keyword recognition. Three locally deployed open-weight LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot inference, followed by external evaluation using independently annotated clinical documentation from MIMIC-IV. ResultsClinStigma-SUD consists of 500 clinician-adjudicated synthetic clinical documentation sentences. Inter-rater agreement was 98.8% across the full benchmark (Cohens {kappa} = 0.976) and 94.0% within the intentionally ambiguous subset ({kappa} = 0.880). Under zero-shot prompting, binary accuracy ranged from 84.8% to 91.8% across evaluated models, while F1 for the ambiguous (gray) class ranged from 0.038 to 0.423. Zero-shot external evaluation on 3,716 annotated examples from the independently annotated Harrigian MIMIC-IV corpus yielded 84.4% accuracy (84.4% balanced accuracy; macro F1 0.824), against a 69.9% majority-class baseline. Stigmatizing-class F1 was 0.879 in the substance-related subgroup and 0.883 in the full external corpus. Discussion and ConclusionClinStigma establishes a reproducible clinician-guided framework for developing synthetic evaluation benchmarks for contextual clinical language. By combining structured clinical expertise, explicit annotation guidance, synthetic benchmark generation, and external evaluation, the framework enables open, privacy-preserving evaluation of language models while providing a scalable foundation for benchmark development across additional clinical specialties, including obstetrics, emergency medicine, and mental health.

papers.title: From examinations to consultations: a physician-reviewed Japanese benchmark for large language models in traditional Kampo medicine
papers.abstract: ObjectivesPatients and clinicians increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) about Kampo, Japans traditional medicine. Yet evaluations of LLMs have measured accuracy on examination questions, which ask what a model knows; a consultation asks whether it can apply that knowledge to the patient at hand. No benchmark had measured that. Materials and MethodsKampoBench comprises 74 consultation scenarios and 310 conversation-specific rubric criteria, following the design of HealthBench. Scenarios, criteria and reference answers were drafted by an LLM and revised by board-certified Kampo physicians. Ten current models from three vendors were evaluated. Because LLM graders are known to favor their own family, each response was graded by a model from each vendor. ResultsThe best model reached 74.8-86.3% across graders, the physician-revised reference answers 87.9-92.4%. Rankings were stable across graders (Spearmans rho 0.952-0.976), and the family-favoring deviation was 0.4 to 0.6 percentage points, below the bootstrap standard deviation of one measurement; grader leniency varied by 14.3 points. Models were most reliable on criteria about advising that care be sought (83.6%) and least reliable on those requiring a known crude-drug risk to be tied to the case (17.5%), though 79.2% of those responses named the drug. DiscussionThe shortfall lay in applying knowledge to the case rather than in holding it -- a distinction examination-format evaluations cannot make. ConclusionEvaluation in traditional medicine should measure the judgments a consultation requires, not recall alone. Quoted alongside the grader that produced it, a KampoBench score is a usable measure of those judgments. Lay summaryPeople increasingly ask artificial intelligence chatbots about Kampo, the traditional herbal medicine used alongside conventional care in Japan. Earlier tests used examination questions, which check what a chatbot knows. A real consultation asks something harder: whether the chatbot can apply that knowledge to the person asking. We built KampoBench, 74 realistic consultations in Japanese. For each one, specialist Kampo physicians reviewed a list of what a good answer should and should not contain, 310 items in all. We then tested ten current chatbots from three companies. The answers were scored by chatbots, and a chatbot might favor its own companys chatbots, so every answer was scored by one chatbot from each company. No such favoritism was detected, but the scorers differed in strictness. The best chatbot scored 75-86%, depending on the scorer; answers revised by physicians scored 88-92%. The chatbots were good at telling people to seek medical care. They were poor at relating a known risk of an herbal ingredient to the persons situation, such as noticing that two medicines the person already takes contain the same ingredient, often even when they named it. Tests of chatbots in traditional medicine should measure such judgments, not knowledge alone.

papers.title: Do Calibrated-Probability Claims Hold Up in Clinical Diagnosis? A Pre-registered Evaluation of a Decision Model Against Frontier Language Models
papers.abstract: BackgroundA new class of AI "decision models" returns a probability for every option in a single pass and is marketed as calibrated, which invites use in clinical triage. Whether those probabilities hold up on clinical diagnosis has not been independently tested. ObjectiveTo test the diagnostic accuracy, calibration, and probabilistic coherence of a decision model (Jev 1.13, TypeSafe AI) against frontier language models, with and without reasoning. MethodsIn a pre-registered study (OSF, registered 26 September 2026), we compared Jev with Claude Opus 5.5 (adaptive reasoning, always on) and Claude Opus 5 (reasoning disabled) on three case sets: the 45 Semigran symptom-checker vignettes, 1,000 stratified synthetic patients from DDXPlus with reference differentials, and 80 simulated ophthalmic complaints (40 diagnoses at two levels of detail). Each model returned a probability for every diagnosis on a fixed list. Outcomes were top-1 and top-3 accuracy, expected calibration error (ECE), Brier score, the rate of exactly zero probability on the true diagnosis, sensitivity to option order, behavior on uninformative inputs, and behavior when the true diagnosis was absent. ResultsOn DDXPlus, top-1 accuracy was 72.0% for Jev, 79.5% for Opus 5 without reasoning, and 87.4% for Opus 5.5 (both comparisons with Jev P<.001). Jev assigned exactly zero probability to the true diagnosis in 62 of 1,000 cases (6.2%); neither comparator did so in any case. Calibration error did not differ between Jev and the registered comparator (ECE difference 0.007, 95% CI -0.026 to 0.038). Offered an explicit "none of these" option, Jev declined to diagnose all 30 uninformative inputs; without that option, it assigned a mean 58% to a single diagnosis. Order sensitivity was small in all models. Given the option list with no patient information, Jev placed up to 96% on a single diagnosis, while the comparators spread probability almost evenly. On the ophthalmic complaints, accuracy did not differ (Jev 88.8%, Opus 5 91.2%, Opus 5.5 88.8%), and Jev was better calibrated than the registered comparator (ECE difference -0.081, 95% CI -0.124 to -0.018). ConclusionsThe decision model matched frontier models on short, distinctive ophthalmic complaints but fell well behind on multi-symptom synthetic patients, including behind a comparator without reasoning, and there it excluded the correct diagnosis outright in about 1 in 16 cases. Its probabilities signaled uncertainty only when the question offered a way to abstain. Calibration claims for clinical decision models should be tested on clinical tasks, with explicit abstention options and zero-probability rates reported.

papers.title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification
papers.abstract: BackgroundAttention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. MethodsThis study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. ResultsAmong the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. ConclusionsThe proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

papers.title: Digital wellbeing in the social media era: dual pathway analysis of emotional and behavioural distress indicators and public health utility
papers.abstract: Social media language and digital lifestyle behaviours are promoted as scalable signals of population mental health, but predictive models are often evaluated in ways that overstate accuracy. We analysed 20,000 tweets from 72 users, labelled by whether the account belonged to a user identified as depressed, and two synthetic datasets (100,000 and 30,000 records) linking screen time, sleep and social media use with self-reported stress. Under a conventional tweet-level split, a term-weighted logistic regression appeared accurate (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.835), but when whole users were held out its performance fell to near chance (0.595; 95% confidence interval 0.505-0.686), because the model largely recognised users and their topics. Depression-associated tweets were more often negative (31.7% versus 24.2%), yet sentiment alone could not identify unseen users (0.539). The two behavioural datasets gave opposite answers: strong discrimination in one (0.926), driven by short sleep, and chance in the other (0.506), so synthetic results reflect how the data were generated. At a population prevalence of 10%, positive predictive values would be 0.10-0.30. Digital distress signals should be validated across individuals, on real linked data and at realistic prevalence before informing public health surveillance or prevention.

papers.title: Understanding clinician engagement with electronic health records: a mixed-methods study of structured data entry using the Theory of Planned Behaviour
papers.abstract: BackgroundElectronic health records (EHRs) are central to NHS clinical practice, and the value of the data they hold depends on clinicians entering structured data. Structured data entry (SDE) is nonetheless used inconsistently, and most evidence comes from US settings documenting barriers rather than the mechanisms interventions must target. This is, to our knowledge, the first study to apply the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) to SDE, to examine SDE behaviour among UK NHS doctors, and to apply corpus linguistics to clinicians free-text accounts of EHR use. MethodsA two-part mixed-methods study was conducted at a large NHS teaching hospital in central London using the Epic EHR. Study 1 was a cross-sectional survey of non-consultant grade doctors comprising the System Usability Scale (SUS), a purpose-designed TPB questionnaire, and two open-text questions analysed using corpus linguistics. Study 2 was an Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) of semi-structured interviews with six resident doctors. ResultsEighty-three doctors responded; 65 completed the SUS and 49 the TPB questionnaire. Mean SUS score was 62.1 (95% CI 58.3-65.9), below the benchmark of 68 and equivalent to a grade of "D". Structured features were used markedly less often than narrative notes. TPB constructs explained 56% of the variance in intention (F(3,45) = 18.95, p < .001); attitudes (p = .003) and subjective norms (p = .009) predicted intention independently, whereas perceived behavioural control did not (p = .14). Intention predicted self-reported use of problem lists, event-specific templates and standardised documents, but not narrative notes. Corpus analysis identified time pressure and interface friction as dominant barriers. IPA generated four themes: structured documentation as cognitive relief; as fragile collective infrastructure; as a practice clinicians are expected to perform but not enabled to learn; and as a format that can flatten clinical reasoning. ConclusionsEngagement with SDE is driven principally by attitudes and social norms rather than by perceived control, and the barriers clinicians describe arise from the intersection of interface design, training, team norms and institutional expectation. Interventions addressing usability alone are unlikely to succeed: sustained change requires team-level normative reinforcement, specialty-relevant training that explains both how and why, and systems that preserve space for clinical narrative.

papers.title: Dynamic Risk Stratification for Short-Term Deterioration After Acute Stroke: Incremental Value of Radiology-Report-Derived Neuroimaging Phenotypes Beyond Dynamic ICU States, a retrospective cohort study with temporal validation
papers.abstract: BackgroundPrediction models after stroke increasingly add neuroimaging information to bedside data. Whether findings documented in radiology reports improve short-term risk stratification beyond a patients evolving physiological state is unknown. MethodsWe studied 4,827 adults with acute ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage or subarachnoid haemorrhage in MIMIC-IV (2008-2019). At eight landmarks from 6 to 48 hours after ICU admission, models ranked patients by their risk of deterioration or death within 24 hours. The baseline model combined demographic and clinical characteristics, a previously validated dynamic ICU state representation, and the physiology, treatment and imaging status at each landmark. A locally run language model extracted imaging phenotypes from 6,992 head CT and MRI reports; three phenotypes and four location categories met a pre-specified reliability criterion for automated extraction in independent validation and entered the model. The primary outcome was the difference in the proportion of events captured among the 10% of patients ranked highest at each landmark, in temporal validation (2017-2019; 8,923 patient-landmarks, 666 events). ResultsAmong the highest-ranked 10%, adding imaging phenotypes captured no additional event (348 of 666 with and without them): a difference of 0.00 percentage points (95% CI -2.20 to +2.01). Discrimination (AUROC 0.855 vs 0.849), calibration and net benefit were similar. No prespecified sensitivity analysis, stroke subtype or availability-adjusted analysis showed statistically supported incremental capture. In a post hoc redundancy analysis, imaging phenotypes improved capture when added to demographic and clinical characteristics alone (+12.91 points, 7.54 to 17.81), but this gain was no longer evident once the dynamic state representation was included. ConclusionsNeuroimaging phenotypes derived from routine radiology reports were associated with short-term deterioration, but we found no evidence that they added risk stratification value beyond the dynamic ICU state and contemporaneous physiology.

papers.title: Data-efficient machine learning for the detection of duodenal neoplasia: a multi-centre study
papers.abstract: BackgroundMachine Learning (ML) has shown promise in histopathological diagnosis, but rare tumours, like duodenal epithelial neoplasms, are challenging because large, labelled datasets are difficult to assemble. We propose a data-efficient ML pipeline for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia in whole-slide images. MethodsWe assembled a five-hospital dataset of haematoxylin and eosin-stained duodenal biopsy whole slide images (WSIs) at 10x magnification, comprising 8,027 normal and 401 neoplastic biopsies, including adenomas, carcinomas and neuroendocrine tumours. WSIs were divided into patches and encoded using the Hibou-B foundation model. We compared global standardisation with unsupervised site-specific standardisation of patch embeddings. Our pipeline combined principal component analysis, a Gaussian mixture model and a Random Forest classifier. We assessed generalisability using leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation across four hospitals and on an independent test set from a fifth hospital. ResultsIn leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation, the pipeline achieved a mean accuracy of 90%, sensitivity of 96%, specificity of 83% and an AUC of 0.96. On the external test hospital, it achieved 94% accuracy, 93% sensitivity, 95% specificity, and AUC of 0.97. Site-specific standardisation improved mean cross-validation accuracy by 20 percentage points compared with global standardisation, while the Gaussian mixture pipeline improved accuracy by 12 percentage points compared with mean pooling of patch embeddings. ConclusionsWe present a data-efficient ML approach for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia from WSIs. Strong performance was maintained across hospitals and on an independent external test cohort despite the limited number of neoplastic training cases, supporting the feasibility of foundation-model-based approaches for rare histopathological diagnoses.

papers.title: Precision Evidence Bench: Assessing PICO alignment and faithful reporting in clinical AI
papers.abstract: Clinicians routinely make decisions for patients whose comorbidities, prior therapies, laboratory abnormalities, or demographic characteristics are not reflected in the supporting evidence, even though these factors can influence treatment selection. Given this gap in the evidence base, we sought to evaluate how AI models respond to clinical questions in which patient characteristics or the treatment comparison and outcome of interest may affect the applicability of available evidence. We developed and publicly released Precision Evidence Bench, a benchmark of 209 synthetic clinical questions with specified population, intervention, comparator, and outcome (PICO) elements. Each answer is assessed using a five-item rubric that evaluates whether a single cited source matches the PICO and whether the answer faithfully reports its sources. The item verdicts determine one of five ratings, ranging from Precision match to Unsupported claim, without requiring a reference answer. We evaluated four frontier large language models (LLMs) using web search across all 209 questions, then repeated the evaluation with additional access to a corpus of precision evidence-based findings (pEBFs) designed to address these evidence gaps, using two corpus sizes. For every model, Precision match rates increased with the amount of precision evidence available, from 13 to 18% with web search alone to 17 to 28% with 100 million pEBFs and 41 to 56% with 500 million pEBFs. These findings suggest that access to matching evidence is an important determinant of LLM performance on precision medicine questions.

papers.title: Dynamic near-term risk prediction of clinically significant immune-related adverse events using longitudinal electronic health records
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and evaluate a dynamic model that repeatedly estimates the 30-day risk of a first grade [≥]2 immune-related adverse event (irAE) during immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy. Materials and MethodsAdults initiating ICI therapy during 2015-2022 comprised the development cohort; 2023 initiators formed a nonoverlapping internal temporal evaluation cohort. Every 21 days during the first treatment year, models used available EHR information to predict a first structured phenotype-defined grade [≥]2 irAE during the next 30 days. Evaluation included pooled and within-landmark discrimination, precision-recall performance, calibration, and patient-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals. Feature-state ablations and alternative update schedules examined the contribution of dynamic information. ResultsDevelopment included 1,522 patients and 18,744 evaluable landmarks; temporal evaluation included 526 patients and 6,263 landmarks, of which 184 were positive (2.94%). The multiscale XGBoost model achieved pooled AUROC 0.716 (95% CI, 0.676-0.755), AUPRC 0.067, within-landmark AUROC 0.672 (95% CI, 0.631-0.716), Brier score 0.0281, and log loss 0.1245. The time-aware baseline achieved AUROC 0.631 and within-landmark AUROC 0.536. Updated treatment exposure and laboratory trajectories accounted for most of the gain. A complete-state extension achieved AUROC 0.719 and AUPRC 0.073. The 21-day schedule had the highest discrimination among tested cadences. ConclusionLongitudinal EHR updating improved near-term irAE prediction beyond pretreatment characteristics and treatment time. Phenotype adjudication and independent evaluation of calibration, transportability, and clinical utility are needed before implementation.

papers.title: Short Communication: Technological Challenges in Brazilian Healthcare Regulation: Lessons from SUSfacilMG and CORE Saude MG
papers.abstract: BackgroundDigital systems are central to regulating access to care in Brazils Unified Health System (SUS), but fragmented data can hinder coordination. ObjectiveThis study examines the database structure of SUSfacilMG and identifies modernization priorities, using CORE Saude MG as a comparative reference. MethodsWe assessed metadata from 1,586 SUSfacilMG tables, focusing on naming patterns, relationships, and repeated attributes. We then compared architectural features described for CORE Saude MG. ResultsApproximately 40% of the assessed tables repeated descriptive attributes, including patient identifiers, suggesting substantial duplication. Metadata alone cannot establish operational failures, security incidents, or effects on care. ConclusionA phased review of data models, interfaces, and governance is warranted. Standardized exchange, referential integrity, and controlled access should be evaluated alongside service continuity and data quality. Author summaryBrazils public health system relies on digital platforms to organize access to specialized care. In Minas Gerais, SUSfacilMG has supported this process for many years, accumulating adaptations that are reflected in the database structure. We examined the metadata of 1,586 SUSfacilMG tables, focusing on naming patterns, apparent relationships, and recurring descriptive attributes. Approxim 40% of the tables contained recurring patient-related attributes, indicating struc complexity that may complicate data maintenance and system integration. Comparison with published descriptions of CORE Saude MG highlighted opportunities for phased modernization based on shared data structures, interoperability, and governance. Because the analysis was limited to metadata, findings identified structural opportunities rather than evidence of data inconsist security incidents, or effects on patient care.

papers.title: Proteomic Signatures Capture Environmental Exposures Across Diverse Populations
papers.abstract: Environmental exposures shape disease risk, but the generalizability of circulating protein-based readouts of exposures across diverse populations remains unknown. Using plasma proteomic profiles of 5,416 proteins in 10,043 participants from the All of Us Research Program, we evaluated associations with and composite scores of 100+ exposures, spanning adiposity, air pollution, ambient temperature, and substance use. We find that proteomic exposure signatures are largely consistent across populations and socioeconomic strata, with <1% of proteins showing significant cross-population heterogeneity, which included BMI as an exception, with leptin being the most heterogeneous association. Population-specific leptin trajectories adiposity, together with residual leptin-type 2 diabetes associations after BMI adjustment, revealed sex-specific metabolic risk not captured by BMI alone. Aggregated protein scores were largely exposure-specific, but substance-use scores showed cross-prediction and SES scores were broadly associated. PM2.5 protein scores captured within-region exposure variation and outperformed geographic and socioeconomic correlates, but spatial confounders remain embedded within protein-environment associations. Scores trained in UK Biobank transferred to All of Us for biologically proximal exposures, supporting cross-biobank portability. These findings establish plasma proteomics as a scalable framework for exposure measurement across diverse populations, while underscoring that responsible applications require careful consideration of biological context, social patterning, and cohort structure.

papers.title: Sense and Sensibility: Sensible Quality Control and Data Decision-Making in Passive Sensing Data for Adolescent Substance Use Risk Prediction
papers.abstract: BackgroundPassively collected smartphone and wearable data, combined with genomic information, may enable scalable early identification of youth who are at risk for substance use disorder. However, heterogeneous data collected in naturalistic settings limit researcher control over data quality, requiring substantial preprocessing. Data cleaning and feature engineering decisions can meaningfully influence analytic outcomes yet are often minimally described or omitted in published work. ObjectivesWe provide rationales and recommendations for common preprocessing challenges in passive sensing research, including establishing inclusion criteria when "outliers" may reflect true behavioral variability, analyzing differences across smartphone operating systems, handling observations collected outside protocol windows, and engineering features for machine learning applications. MethodsWe illustrate principled approaches to these challenges using smartphone and Fitbit data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive DevelopmentSM Study (ABCD). The sample was drawn from the available half of the year-4 follow-up (data release 5.1; N = 4,754; ages 13-14). ResultsExtreme outlying observations were concentrated among low-engagement participants with few observed days. Smartphone usage among Apple users appeared under-recorded relative to Android users when compared with self-report measures. Fitbit-derived behavior differed systematically between observations collected within versus outside protocol windows. We also identified potential errors in the studys default preprocessing pipeline. ConclusionWe recommend prioritizing person-level inclusion criteria that preserve meaningful behavioral variability, examining temporal distributions rather than assuming observations are exchangeable, and thoroughly investigating and reporting data quality issues. Although illustrated using the ABCD Study, these principles broadly apply to research using smartphones, wearables, and other digital data sources.
